newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ciller presses EU case at NATO meeting.
newsitem.headline: Ciller presses EU case at NATO meeting.

text.p: Turkey pressed its case to its NATO partners on Tuesday to be brought into the mainstream European fold, but stopped short of repeating a threat to veto the alliance's enlargement if it was rebuffed.

NATO officials said Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller used a special NATO ministerial meeting with new U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to underline Ankara's view that NATO and European Union enlargement were linked.
"The enlargement of the European Union and the enlargement of NATO go hand in hand," Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini quoted Ciller as saying.

Ciller has horrified Ankara's partners in the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation over the past month by suggesting that Turkey would veto NATO enlargement if it was not allowed to join the 15-nation European Union.
The EU -- like NATO, set to enlarge into eastern Europe -- has no plans to offer memberhip to Turkey in the near term.

Ciller has also threatened to use Turkey's NATO veto to bloc the use of NATO weaponry by the Western European Union (WEU), the nascent European defence arm, unless it is given a deciding role in the grouping.

At a news conference following the NATO meeting, Albright said the issue of Turkey had been high on the agenda of talks she had held during her whirlwind European tour that has already taken in France and Germany.
"We have talked about the importance of having Turkey anchored to the West, a secular Turkey," Albright said.
She added that it would be well for Turkey to recognise that NATO enlargement was in its interest.
NATO officials have expressed frustration over Turkey's demands.

"It is not in our hands to solve a problem of the European Union," NATO Secretary General Javier Solana told a news conference, noting that Turkey has voted with the rest of NATO to begin the enlargement process.
Turkey has had an association agreement with the European Union since 1963 and filed a formal application to join in 1987.
Since then, however, its has seen a stream of eastern European countries put on the fast track to EU membership while its own application has languished.
It has been put on hold by EU concerns over human rights and an unspoken question about whether the Union wants to incorporate a large Moslem state into its ranks.
